html:
The Indian Slavery Act of 1843 was a law passed by the East India Company that took away the legal standing of slavery in the lands it ruled in India.

Britain's Slavery Abolition Act of 1833 had left out the Company's territories, where many people were held as slaves: farm labourers tied to landowners, household servants, people sold in famines.

The act did not free anyone outright. Instead it said that:

  • No court could enforce a claim of ownership over a person.
  • No one could be taken from someone else's control on the grounds that they were a slave.
  • Harm done to a slave was punished just as harm to a free person.

In practice this meant a slave could walk away, but many had nowhere to go. The Indian Penal Code of 1860 went further and made buying, selling or holding slaves a crime.

Unfree labour lived on in other forms, above all debt bondage, which independent India banned again in 1976. In the same decades, the end of slavery elsewhere fed the system of Indian indenture.
sum: The Indian Slavery Act of 1843 was a law passed by the East India Company that took away the legal standing of slavery in the lands it ruled in India.
